items.stem: A program shows a subtotal of 123 for 3 milk teas at 120 pesos, and the total at the end is also wrong. A teammate rewrites the last step. Why is that a poor choice?

options.text: The subtotal is the first wrong value, so the cause is in step 3.
options.feedback: Changing a later step hides the symptom and leaves the cause in place.

options.text: The last step is always correct, so nobody should edit it.
options.feedback: Last steps can be wrong. In this program an earlier step caused the error.

options.text: Rewriting any step always breaks the whole program.
options.feedback: Rewriting is fine when it changes the step that caused the error.

items.stem: A fix makes 3 teas at 120 pesos total 324, as expected, and the developer ships it. Later a customer buys 2 teas at 150 pesos, pays exactly 300 and gets no discount. Which test would have caught this?

options.text: An order of 50 teas at 120 pesos.
options.feedback: A large order is over 300 and gets the discount under either comparison. The mistake sits at exactly 300.

options.text: An order that totals exactly 300 pesos.
options.feedback: The rule says 300 or more. Only a test at 300 shows whether step 4 includes it.

options.text: A second order of 3 teas at 120 pesos.
options.feedback: That repeats a case that already passed.

items.stem: A developer fixes a failing test by typing that order's expected total into the program. The test now passes. What is the problem?

options.text: The program gets longer and harder to read.
options.feedback: Length is a small cost. The steps are still wrong.

options.text: The test will fail again the next time someone runs it.
options.feedback: The test passes every time. The trouble is every other order.

options.text: Other orders still get a wrong total, so the bug remains.
options.feedback: Typing in one answer satisfies one test and leaves the steps wrong.

items.stem: An AI assistant writes a discount function and says it works. You have 30 seconds before it goes live. What is the best use of the time?

options.text: Read the function's name and trust what it says it does.
options.feedback: A name describes what the author meant. The steps decide the result.

options.text: Ask the assistant a second time whether the code works.
options.feedback: A second answer from the same source is not a test.

options.text: Read the code once from top to bottom.
options.feedback: Reading can miss a boundary. Running a case shows the result.

options.text: Run a normal order, an empty order and an order of exactly 300.
options.feedback: Three quick cases cover a typical input, an empty input and a boundary, where mistakes often sit.
